questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
questions.problem: Find a basis of $\,\text{Ker}(T)$ given that $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}-9x-3y \\ -12x-4y\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Finding the kernel of $\,T\,$ is equivalent to finding the null space of the standard matrix of $\,T.$

For the given linear transformation, the standard matrix is $T=[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 \\ -12 & -4\end{aligned}].$

Setting $x=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}],$ we then need to solve the equation $Tx=0.$ First, we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 \\ -12 & -4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-\frac{4}{3}){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-9 & -3 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The basic variables are the variables whose coefficients are pivots. In this case, the basic variable is $x$, and we have one free variable, $y.$ That means we need to find $x$ in terms of $y.$

From the first equation, we get 

$$
x=-\frac{1}{3}y.
$$

 

Therefore, if $x\in \text{Ker}(T),$ then 

$$
x=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3}y \\ y\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}]y,\,y\in R.
$$

This implies that $B={[\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{3} \\ 1\end{aligned}]}$ is a basis of $\text{Ker}(T).$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
questions.problem: Given the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x+2y \\ 4y+3x\end{aligned}],$ find  $2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-1.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] & {R}_{2} & :={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has no non-pivot column. Therefore, $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=0.$

Finally, we obtain

$$
2\cdot \text{nullity}(T)-1=2\cdot 0-1=-1.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Component of a Vector in the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
questions.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}10x+6y \\ 25x+15y\end{aligned}]$ and the vector $\,u=[\begin{aligned}k \\ 5\end{aligned}].$ Find the value of $\,k\,$ such that $\,u\in \text{Ker}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

So, we need to solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(u) & =0 \\ [\begin{aligned}10\cdot k+6\cdot 5 \\ 25\cdot k+15\cdot 5\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}10k+30 \\ 25k+75\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}10k+30=0 \\ 25k+75=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to both of these equations is $k=-3.$

questions.knowledge_point: Calculating a Component of a Vector in the Kernel of a Linear Transformation
questions.problem: Consider the linear transformation $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3x+y+3z \\ 2x+y+z \\ x-y+5z\end{aligned}]$ and the vector $\,u=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3 \\ k\end{aligned}].$ Find the value of $\,k\,$ such that $\,u\in \text{Ker}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
A vector $u$ belongs to the kernel of a linear transformation $T$ if $T(u)=0.$ 

So, we need to solve the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}T(u) & =0 \\ [\begin{aligned}3\cdot (-2)+3+3\cdot k \\ 2\cdot (-2)+3+k \\ -2-3+5\cdot k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\ [\begin{aligned}-3+3k \\ -1+k \\ -5+5k\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get the system

$$
{\begin{aligned}-3+3k=0 \\ -1+k=0 \\ -5+5k=0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solution to all three of these equations is $k=1.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Nullity of a Linear Transformation
questions.problem:
Given the linear transformation
 $T:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y \\ z\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}3y-x-4z \\ 2x+7z-6y \\ 16z+4x-12y\end{aligned}],$ find $\text{nullity}(T).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we write down the standard matrix of $T:$

$$
T=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 2 & -6 & 7 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}]
$$

Recall that $\text{nullity}(T)=\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)).$

In order to find $\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T)),$ we reduce $T$ to row echelon form, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}T & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 2 & -6 & 7 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 4 & -12 & 16\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+4{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & -4 \\ 0 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

The reduced matrix above has $1$ non-pivot columns (the 2nd one).  Therefore, 

$$
\text{nullity}(T)=\text{dim}(\text{Null}(T))=1.
$$
